sections.content: The course covers real numbers, sequences and series, limits, continuity and differentiation. The content is quite theoretical and proof-based, so it can be challenging if you are not familiar with rigorous mathematical proofs. Keeping up with the lectures and doing exercises regularly is important.
sections.teaching: The instructor explains the main definitions and proofs carefully, and the lecture notes are useful for reviewing. The pace can be quite fast, especially when several new theorems and proof techniques are introduced within a short period of time.
sections.grading: There are regular online quizzes and homework assignments, together with a midterm and a final exam. The course uses two grading schemes and takes the better result. The midterm is closed-book and closed-notes, so understanding the definitions and proof methods is important.
sections.workload: The workload is moderate to high. There is usually a quiz after each lecture and homework every few weeks. Besides completing the assignments, additional time is needed to read the textbook and practice proofs, especially before the exams.

sections.content: Classic real analysis—sequences, limits, continuity, derivatives, integrals. All proofs, no computation. The progression made sense, though the last unit on integration felt a bit rushed.
sections.teaching: He's basically writing the PPT down again; you'd better learn it yourself and go through the proof with him. But feel free to ask him questions.
sections.grading: Fair and transparent. Exams match the homework difficulty. If you want to get a good score, you should follow the proof step by step and show your logic.
sections.workload: Heavy but reasonable. The assignment includes a good amount of proof, and there are lots of extra self-practice exercises you can try. But the effort pays off.

sections.content:
I will try to be as unbiased as possible in making this review.

That being said, some other review on ust.space for 25/26 spring said that he gave readable lecture notes......but I couldn't disagree more. As someone who took MATH 1014 L1, I was somewhat confused multiple times when I self studied this course (because I did not came to lectures, read "TEACHING section" to understand why I didn't). This was mainly because he had made so many typos on his notes, not language typos, but mathematical typos (on his proofs and examples). I had to ask gemini/claude, and other friends multiple times just to confirm whether I was really true or not, and most of the time.....I was. I will place some examples from his notes showing where he was wrong (or typo'ed) in the attachment section. I couldn't be bothered to ask him or the TAs again and again because there were too many typos.

Other than that, everything was covered on this course, except improper integrals (refer to the usual 2033 list of topics). But, maybe because I had already taken L1 for calculus, I learnt nothing new except from the rigor of the logic behind some theorems.
sections.teaching:
I am not going to lie.......I only came full-time for his lectures for the first two lectures of the semester, purely because I do not like his teaching, and I almost never do this for any of my courses. This is because he uses small writing on his lectures, and the voice he uses to teach is very small as well.

After the first lecture of the semester, I told him to change his teaching style, maybe by making the writing larger......or the voice louder. He agreed to me at the time, but the next day.....he did nothing different. I took offense after this, and did not bother coming to lecture anymore.

Sometime before the midterm, he opened a section called "suggestions." I did not add anything, but I expected him to change his teaching style sometime after this, so I attended one lecture after the midterm break. However, i came dissapointed again.......because he did not change the overall parts that I had complained about in the beginning.

I have nothing to say about the TAs, at least they tried to teach, I cannot say the same for the professor however.
sections.grading:
I am not a perfect student, but I expected more from the professor in terms of fairness.

A bit about the grading scheme of this course (No stats were given by the professor):

15% homework (Me: 80/80)
10% midterm exam (online, 1 hr, 4 long questions) (Me: 44/50)
75% exam (offline, 2hrs, 7 long questions) (Me: 73/100)

Homework Comments: Not much to say, it was actually doable, and he only graded specific questions in every homework, but would deduct points if you did not attempt all questions. Was supposed to be 5 homeworks, but he made it 4 due to scheduling issues.

Midterm Comments: I have no excuses for the midterm exam, it was doable and I could have gotten full marks if I hadn't made some misreading issue, making me lose 6 pts.

The only thing I could complain about was that lots of people I knew (and probably people I don't know) were cheating to get 100% because it was an online exam, which is very possible tbh (even tho it was already a bit too easy to begin with).

Final Exam Comments (the thing that made me give an E grading):

I have no gripes against the questions available itself, it was within reach, and I was expecting ~85ish (I blamed myself because I was juggling MATH 2033, and 5 other midterms on the same week). But, when I got back my paper, I was given a 72 mark paper, which was interesting, but not an issue for me. Because of this, I came to paper checking session, 3 days after the exam was held.

Note that when we notice some grading miscalculations during the paper checking session, we could complain about the grading, but they WOULD NOT ADD the points in front of us. The TA had told me they would REGRADE EVEYTHING AGAIN while consulting with other TAs and the professor (behind our backs). The main issue with that? well, I noticed I was deducted for ~8 points for no reasons, 5 points of which even the TA which was in charge of the paper checking session, but did not grade my paper, agreed that I should be awarded said 5 points, because my proofs and solutions had been logical. Hence, I had asked the TA if I could regrade all 8 points, because all 8 of them stemmed from possible correct answers (which was the TA's own words btw)

6-7 hours later (long after the paper checking session ended), I had noticed I only got an additional 1 point for my paper. So, I asked the professor why I had only gotten 1 point when I appealed for 8 points, and which of the questions I appealed for was given the point. His reply? "I have reviewed all the cases where scores need to be adjusted. I believe your score is correct and the decision is final."

At this point, I have accepted my fate, and could not be bothered to further debate the professor on the grading.

P.S. I got B+ for a weighted average of 78.55. My friend got A- for around 81. So I guess the cutoff for A range is 80?

Overall, I am content with B+, but I could've gotten A- if the grading were more "fair" to begin with. Ofc, this is just my opinion.

The author likes to skip steps, does not provide the intuitive idea on how to prove the theorems and just throws the proof at your face, expecting you to understand it.
Also one more comment on his notes. The notes is just screenshots of theorems and examples of the book. And then XMS writes the exact same proof of the book onto his ipad. Yeah guys. We paid college tuition for this guy to read a book to us. Yeah I can't read printed english text. I absolutely needed his hadnwritten math symbols or else I can't understand anything. Thanks XMS.

Disclaimer: I am a “retaker” of Math2033 since I get failed by Albert Ku in the previous semester.

For new math majors, this is probably the first course for you to explore what is Math and there is still long way to go after this course…good luck.

Prof Hu made a very colorful lecture note with listing every definitions and everything is pretty clear unlike Albert Ku’s messy lecture note with weird order of the content. Anyway, Prof Hu’s content is referred to the Baby Rudin. There’s around 10 exercises at the end of each chapter and 8 concept checking questions.

Chapter 0. Mathematical Argument
5 pages manual telling you how to write a proof.
(won’t teach)

Chapter 1. Number System
Definition of sets, sup and inf, Archimedean Property, Absolute value, norm, CS Inequality

Chapter 2. Basic Topology (probably the most challenging chapter for this course)
Injective, surjective, bijective, union and intersection, countability, defining every terms related to subset in R: complement, neighborhood, open/closed, limit point, perfect, bounded, closure, dense, interior, connected, compact,…

Chapter 3. Sequence and Series
Convergent sequences, subsequence, cauchy sequences, monotonic sequence, upper/lower limit, definition of convergent series, cauchy criterion, convergent tests (this chapter isn’t that detailed since it should be explained in Math3033)

Chapter 4. Continuity
Introducing power function, radical function, exponential function, log function, sin/cos function, rigorous definition of limit, limit at infinity, definition of continuity, uniformly continuous, discontinuity, Intermediate Value Thm, Bolzano thm
(just make sure you know how to write things in epsilon delta language, familiar with the property of continuity and how to use IVT then that’s it)

Chapter 5. Differentiation
Definition of derivative, differentiability, Mean Value Theorem, L’Hopital Rule, Taylor’s Theorem
(Need to know the characteristics of differentiability, how to use MVT and also Taylor’s thm)

Chapter 6. Riemann Integral
Integrability : Partition, Riemann Sum, refinement
Integrability criterion
Property of the Riemann Integral
Leibniz Formula
(This chapter is pretty short, Albert Ku covered way more than Prof Hu)

sections.workload:
The types of problems in exams are nearly fixed. Get more experiences and learn more tricks to solve problems will help you in final. Also be careful.
Presentation: Groups are formed by 1 to 3 persons. Each group is assigned several questions. They will present the question in tutorial by projecting their solutions on the screen as well as telling the TA explanations. If you get stuck with the question, you are allowed to ask the TA.
Therefore, the workload is not high.
